title: Scientific American Magazine Publishes Article by Respected Journalist on Study Showing Brain Changes Came Before Not After “Drug” Use. Difficult to Ignore.

content_html_sanitized:
I reported on this study last week, Questions About Addictions and Mental Illness. Confusing Cause and Effect., based on an article in Reason Magazine, with the subtitle, “Researchers argue that ‘we may need to reevaluate the causal assumptions that underlie brain disease models of addiction.’

 

My response was “Fat Chance! This study is a mortal threat to the pseudoscience of the addiction industry.” Indeed it is.

 

However, the publication of this article in Scientific American magazine makes it difficult to ignore.

 

See“Addiction Risk Shows up in Children’s Brain Scans before Drug Use Starts, Brain differences in children and teens who experiment with drugs early show up before they take their first puff or sip”, by Maia Szalavitz. She is the author of Undoing Drugs: How Harm Reduction Is Changing the Future of Drugs and Addiction.

 

She is also a contributing opinion writer for the New York Times and author or co-author of seven other books.”)

 

Obviously, she is someone difficult to ignore.

 

It is the complaint and purpose of MarijuanaNews.com to urge journalists to fulfill the obligations of journalism and report something beyond telling us that average THC levels have increased since Woodstock. OMG! OMG!

 

And this study has real world consequences.

 

“Five years later, students at the schools that did use the program had 87 percent lower odds of developing substance use disorders. “It’s a 35 percent reduction in the annual growth of substance use disorders across time,” says Patricia Conrod, a professor of psychiatry at the University of Montreal and lead author of the prevention trial. The results were published in the American Journal of Psychiatry in January.

Conrod emphasizes that “risky” traits have pluses as well as minuses. For example, a tendency to seek new experiences can be critical for success in science, medicine and the arts. A willingness to take risks is useful in occupations ranging from firefighting to entrepreneurship. The trick is to help young people manage such predilections safely.

In some children she has worked with, who start drugs as early as age 13, Conrod says that “the drive to self-medicate is so strong; it’s really striking. There really is this discomfort with their inner world.” As a result, providing ways to manage these feelings without misusing drugs—and without pathologizing those with outlying traits—can be a powerful way to support healthy development.”

Think of the children???
